summary: Describes how to build an IP echo host, which sends back IP datagrams after swapping the source and destination addresses. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Throw a ball at a wall and it comes back to you. An echo host bounces your message back.

questions: what is an ip echo host
subtitle: A host that bounces IP datagrams back to their sender by reversing addresses.

tldr.problem: Developers need a way to test protocols and applications over a real network without distributing test software to many machines.
tldr.mechanism: An IP echo host receives any IP datagram sent to it and returns the same datagram to the original source, with the source and destination addresses swapped.
tldr.outcome: This allows developers to create looped-back conversations across the real Internet to expose their code to actual network conditions, but poses security risks if not carefully deployed.

facts.label: Core operation
facts.value: Swap source and destination IP addresses

today: RFC 2075 is Experimental and remains historical documentation of a testing technique that was valuable in IP's early days but is rarely deployed in modern networks due to security concerns and the availability of better testing tools.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2075 describes the concept of the IP echo host, a tool that was heavily used in the 1970s and 1980s but had fallen out of favor by the time this memo was written. An IP echo host receives an IP datagram addressed to it, swaps the source and destination IP addresses, and sends the datagram back to its original sender.

The effect is that the datagram appears to originate from the echo host, creating a loop. This is tremendously useful for debugging applications and protocols because developers can expose their traffic to the real Internet—with its congestion, cross traffic, and variable delays—without having to deploy prototype software to many test machines.
sections.eli5: Imagine a special computer that catches every message you send it and throws it right back at you with the addresses flipped. That is an IP echo host.

sections.title: Basic Operation
sections.content:
When an echo host receives a simple IP datagram with no options and a protocol field other than ICMP (1), it performs a straightforward sequence: swap the source and destination IP addresses, decrement the Time-To-Live (TTL) field by one, recalculate the IP header checksum, and transmit the modified datagram back to the original sender.

If the TTL reaches zero after decrementing, the datagram must not be echoed. The RFC also requires that echo hosts perform the same sanity checks that a normal IP router would perform before accepting a datagram.
sections.eli5: Flip the 'from' and 'to' addresses, count down a hop counter so it does not loop forever, and send it back.

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.content:
IP datagrams often carry options that complicate echoing. For example, source route options must be reversed when echoed. Timestamp options require careful handling to maintain consistency with the new source and destination addresses while preserving information about the path traveled.

ICMP datagrams should generally not be echoed, because they usually indicate a problem encountered by an earlier echoed datagram. However, certain ICMP messages (such as those related to MTU discovery) may be safely echoed in specific situations.
sections.eli5: Some messages have extra instructions inside them. The echo host has to understand these and update them so they still make sense after the flip.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
Echo hosts create significant security hazards. A malicious sender can forge the source address of a datagram to point at a third party, causing the echo host to send datagrams to that third party. More seriously, if an echo host is placed inside a firewall, attackers outside the firewall can exploit it to inject packets that appear to originate from inside.

Address spoofing can also be used for flooding attacks: if an attacker sends datagrams to one echo host with the source address of another echo host, the two hosts will exchange datagrams in a loop. Although the TTL requirement limits this damage, the memo recommends never placing echo hosts inside firewalls and using rate limiting to protect against flooding.
sections.eli5: A bad person can lie about who they are and trick the echo host into sending messages to innocent people. This is dangerous, so echo hosts should only be used with care.
